$schema-note: Hand-maintained. Data, not code: nothing under src/ imports this file.
purpose: The guard ledger for WIN-258 TRANCHE 5 — `eventing`'s canonical store, the
THIRTEENTH owner behind the one PostgreSQL client ADR M0.3 §15 gives the
ORM, and the SMALLEST: one row. One entry per guard: per scope predicate,
per shape check that stands where a migration-only CHECK stands, per parse
that stands where the column constrains nothing, and per clause of the
containment join the erasure path depends on. Each carries the file it
lives in, the EXACT text that implements it (`from`), the edit that removes
it (`to`), and the NAMED cases that were seen to go red (`kills`).
IT IS AN ELEVENTH FILE beside mutations.json, mutations-identity.json,
mutations-ports.json, mutations-outbox.json, mutations-tools.json,
mutations-agents.json, mutations-cost.json, mutations-channels.json,
mutations-governance.json, mutations-secrets.json, mutations-providers.json,
mutations-conversations.json, mutations-skills.json and
mutations-memory.json rather than an extension of any of them, for the
reason the fourth was: each tranche is a separate claim about a separate
port surface, and a reader checking one should not have to read past the
others. All are hashed by the same packages.adapters.config rule and counted
together by the v1 ledger.
WHY ONE ROW NEEDED A SWEEP OF ITS OWN. `NotificationRule` has NINE columns
and the database constrains almost none of what matters in them.
`filters` and `delivery` are JSONB behind ONE check each, and both are on
the ROOT — `jsonb_typeof(...) = 'object'` — so no field inside either is
checked at all. `name` is a plain TEXT with no length constraint, and
`domain/rule-name.ts` says outright that its 1-120 bound therefore IS the
constraint. `createdBy` is a plain TEXT. A store that CAST any of the three
would hand `ruleAdmits` a filter with no patterns, the delivery adapter a
kind outside the union, or a caller a `RuleName` that is not one.
AND THE TENANCY COLUMN IS ONE WHERE THE AGGREGATE CARRIES THREE. The row
stores `environmentId` and nothing else; `NotificationRule.scope` is a whole
`EnvironmentScope`. Every read echoes the caller's triple rather than
selecting it, which is truthful only because `scopedWhere` walks the whole
ancestry — the legacy `environmentScopeWhere` does the same. Three of the
entries below are the three conjuncts of that walk, and three more are the
three clauses of the erasure's containment join.
SEVEN NAMED CASES EXIST BECAUSE THIS LEDGER WAS ENUMERATED FIRST. Five
guards had no case anywhere that could go red: the PROJECT clause of the
erasure join (one project held every row the organization held), the
`createdBy` clause (one operator held every rule), the ENVIRONMENT clause
(the scenario only ever erased at the organization), the NUL guard on the
`findRuleByName` LOOKUP, and the NUL guard on the erasure's REPLACEMENT.
Two more were found the same way: `updateRule` addressed with another
environment's scope, and the two vacuous-selector short-circuits, which are
indistinguishable from falling through to a query that answers zero anyway
unless the STATEMENT COUNT is what is pinned.
procedure: PROVE THE SUITES GREEN FIRST. Tranche 1's first sweep reported 22 kills and
every one was VACUOUS: a context's `dist` had been cleaned, so every suite
failed to load its import and would have 'died' against any mutation at
all, including none. The driver runs each suite set UNMUTATED and refuses
to sweep unless it is green with a non-zero executed case count, and
classifies a run with no executed cases as VACUOUS rather than as a kill.
THE INTEGRATION SUITES RUN ON A REAL POSTGRESQL, in a container, on the
machine that has a daemon. `eventing-rows.test.ts` is the only suite here
that runs without one, and it is the one that reaches the branches a
container suite cannot: a container only ever reads rows THIS BINARY WROTE,
so the three unreadable-row arms are unreachable from one except through
the rows `eventing-rules.integration.test.ts` plants as raw SQL — and the
two `*_json_root` guards are unreachable from ANY suite through the port,
because `toRuleFilterInput` and `toDestinationInput` return objects on every
path the domain can build.
THE ADAPTER'S SUITES RUN FROM SOURCE, so a mutation needs no rebuild. Only
the CONTEXT's `dist` is imported through a package entry point, and no
mutation below touches a context. That is why the driver can apply, run and
restore in one pass rather than rebuilding forty times — and it is also why
the driver checks the file back to byte-identical after each restore.
EVERY `from` IS A UNIQUE SUBSTRING OF ITS FILE and is applied literally, so
a mutation that failed to match is reported as UNAPPLIED rather than
scored as a survivor.

mutations.name: M-V01 rows: NotificationRule.name is parsed, not cast
mutations.note: `name` is a plain TEXT with NO length constraint; `domain/rule-name.ts` says the 1-120 predicate IS the constraint. A cast hands a caller a `RuleName` that is not one, and the value flows straight into the `@@unique([environmentId, name])` lookup.

mutations.name: M-V02 rows: NotificationRule.filters is parsed, not cast
mutations.note: The refusal must name the COLUMN and carry its own code, or an operator reading a log cannot find the row. Changing the column name is the smallest edit that keeps the refusal and destroys its usefulness.

mutations.name: M-V03 rows: an unparseable filters column REFUSES rather than returning empty
mutations.note: `NotificationRule_filters_json_root` checks the ROOT only, so `{}` is a legal row this binary cannot read. A cast puts an object with no `eventPatterns` into `ruleAdmits`, whose first act is to iterate them.

mutations.name: M-V04 rows: an unrecognised delivery type REFUSES rather than passing through
mutations.note: `domain/destination.ts` says its default arm exists so that "a rule whose destination cannot be parsed is skipped at routing time rather than delivered to an unknown place". A cast deletes that arm.

mutations.name: M-V05 rows: scopedWhere narrows on the ENVIRONMENT
mutations.note: Without the leaf column every rule of every environment in the project is visible from every other one. The double enforces scope isolation, so this is a divergence the differential sees.

mutations.name: M-V06 rows: scopedWhere narrows on the PROJECT
mutations.note: The clause that makes the ECHOED scope truthful. Without it a caller holding the right environment id under the wrong project gets a rule tagged with an ancestry it does not have.

mutations.name: M-V07 rows: scopedWhere narrows on the ORGANIZATION
mutations.note: The outermost conjunct of the ancestry walk the legacy `environmentScopeWhere` performs.

mutations.name: M-V08 rows: a PROJECT-level erasure selector still carries its organization
mutations.note: A project id alone would reach a project of ANOTHER organization. Project ids are uuids so a collision is not the risk; a caller passing a project it does not own is.

mutations.name: M-V09 rows: tenantWhere's ENVIRONMENT arm is the full scoped predicate
mutations.to: if (scope.level === "environment") return { environment: { project: { organizationId: scope.organizationId } } };
mutations.note: An environment-level count that widened to the organization would report a plan far larger than the erasure it precedes, and `privacy` renders that plan to an operator before they consent.

mutations.name: M-V10 guards: a non-uuid identifier is refused

export function guardUuid(label: string, value: string): void {
  if (!UUID.test(value)) {
mutations.to:
export function guardUuid(label: string, value: string): void {
  if (false) {
mutations.note: The context's own `SequenceIdGenerator` mints `id-0001` and `testEnvironmentScope()` mints `org-1`/`proj-1`/`env-1`; all four are accepted by the double and refused by `@db.Uuid`, and every use-case suite in the context passes with them.

mutations.name: M-V11 guards: the uuid predicate is ANCHORED at both ends
mutations.note: An unanchored pattern admits `{...}`, which PostgreSQL's own `uuid` input accepts and stores under a DIFFERENT spelling — so a row would be written under one string and read back under another, and every rule-id comparison in this context is a string comparison in TypeScript.

mutations.name: M-V12 guards: guardScope checks the ORGANIZATION id
mutations.note: An organization-level erasure selector names ONE id, and it is this one. Skipping it would send `org-1` into a `@db.Uuid` comparison inside the caller's multi-context erasure transaction.

mutations.name: M-V13 guards: guardScope checks the PROJECT id
mutations.note: The middle conjunct of the ancestry filter, and the one no environment-level caller can reach through a scope it did not build itself.

mutations.name: M-V14 guards: guardScope checks the ENVIRONMENT id
mutations.note: The leaf id, which is also the only tenancy COLUMN the row carries.

mutations.name: M-V15 guards: a NUL byte in a text value is refused
mutations.note: PostgreSQL cannot store U+0000 in a TEXT column or inside a jsonb string, and NOTHING in this context refuses one: `parseRuleName` trims nothing and bounds by code units, `nonEmptyString` asks only for length, and the email rule really is just "contains @".

mutations.name: M-V16 guards: an Invalid Date is refused before it reaches timestamp(3)
mutations.note: `createNotificationRule` and `editNotificationRule` stamp both instants from the context's `Clock`, and a clock that answers `new Date(NaN)` produces a driver error naming neither the column nor the port call.

mutations.name: M-V17 guards: the DELIVERY union's url arm is walked for NULs
mutations.note: Each arm of the destination union carries exactly one string and each is a TEXT-shaped value inside the `delivery` JSONB. The url arm is the one the SSRF screen also looks at, so it is the one an operator is most likely to paste into.

mutations.name: M-V18 guards: the filters JSON root is checked
mutations.note: Restates `NotificationRule_filters_json_root`. UNREACHABLE through the port — `toRuleFilterInput` returns an object on every path — so the case calls it directly, which is the only honest way to build the input.

mutations.name: M-V19 guards: the delivery JSON root is checked, under its OWN code
mutations.note: TWO CHECKS, TWO CODES. `NotificationRule_filters_json_root` and `NotificationRule_delivery_json_root` are separate constraints on separate columns, and a shared code would make an operator read one incident as the other.

mutations.name: M-V20 guards: the LOOKUP name is guarded, not only the written one
mutations.note: `findRuleByName` sends the name as a bind parameter of a SELECT, and a NUL in a bind parameter is refused before any row is compared — inside whatever transaction the caller has open. Guarding only the write path keeps the 25P02 out of an insert and lets a lookup put it there instead.

mutations.name: M-V21 guards: the erasure REPLACEMENT is guarded like any other text
mutations.note: The replacement comes from the CALLER — the erasure target passes a fixed sentinel, but the port does not require one — and it lands in a TEXT column inside the multi-context transaction `privacy` opened. It is the one place in this store where a refusal costs somebody else's work.

mutations.name: M-V22 refusal: a TransactionScopeError is RETHROWN, not turned into a Result
mutations.note: The three scope refusals are the property tranche 1 built. Converting them to a `Result` would let a use case that lost its transaction carry on as though a row had merely failed to write.

mutations.name: M-V23 refusal: a foreign key violation gets its OWN reason code
mutations.note: "that environment does not exist" and "a table is down" are separate incidents behind one published code, so the distinction lives in `details.reason` — and a reason that fell back to the driver's own message would name neither.

mutations.name: M-V24 refusal: a refusal's reason LEADS with its distinct code
mutations.note: `domain/errors.ts` mints ONE code for a store failure, so the only thing separating five guards in a log is the code at the front of the reason string.

mutations.name: M-V25 refusal: a name clash is recognised by the ORM's own code
mutations.note: `register-notification-rule.ts` says a racing insert "still fails at the store, where the adapter maps it onto the same code". The driver's raw 23505 message names the KEY COLUMNS and not the index, which is why this is recognised by `P2002` rather than by matching prose.

mutations.name: M-V26 rules: every read is SCOPED
mutations.note: The port's own instruction: "There is no findRule(id). There is findRule(scope, id), and an implementation MUST return null — not a row from another environment — when the id exists elsewhere."

mutations.name: M-V27 rules: insertRule writes the DOMAIN's id, not the column default
mutations.note: `NotificationRule.id` has `@default(uuid())`, so omitting it writes a row the caller cannot address: `registerNotificationRule` returns the rule it built and the store would have stored a different one.

mutations.name: M-V28 rules: only a NAME CLASH is turned into a conflict on insert
mutations.note: The catch sits over EVERY driver failure the insert can raise, and the foreign key is one of them. Swallowing it would report "that name is taken" for an environment that does not exist.

mutations.name: M-V29 rules: updateRule is addressed by the whole ancestry, not by the id
mutations.note: The legacy `updateRule` writes with an UNSCOPED where and is safe only because of the read before it. Here the scope travels on the rule, so a synthesised one must match no row rather than update somebody else's.

mutations.name: M-V30 rules: an update that matched NOTHING is reported, not invented
mutations.note: `updateManyAndReturn` answers an empty array rather than raising, so without this the method would return the row it did not write — which is exactly the upsert the in-memory double performs and this store deliberately does not.

mutations.name: M-V31 rules: updatedAt is written EXPLICITLY, against the @updatedAt stamp
mutations.note: The column carries `@updatedAt`, so the client stamps it on every update unless a value is supplied — and `editNotificationRule` already computed one from the context's Clock. Letting the client win makes `updateNotificationRule` return a rule that disagrees with the row it just wrote.

mutations.name: M-V32 rules: deleteRule reports whether a row actually went
mutations.note: `deleteNotificationRule` turns the boolean into the caller's answer, so a store that always said `true` would report a rule removed from an environment that never held it.

mutations.name: M-V33 rules: the DELETE is scoped
mutations.note: An unscoped delete addressed by id alone removes another environment's standing order, and the caller is told it succeeded.

mutations.name: M-V34 rules: listRules is NEWEST FIRST
mutations.note: The port promises it and the legacy `orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" }` is where it comes from. The double sorts the same way, so the differential compares two ordered lists rather than two sets.

mutations.name: M-V35 rules: the routing read is narrowed to ENABLED rules in the STORE
mutations.note: The port says why: "a routing pass over a busy environment must not load every disabled rule to discard it in memory". `ruleAdmits` re-checks `enabled`, so the delivery would still be correct and the read would still be wrong.

mutations.name: M-V36 erasure: a vacuous selector costs NO statement on the count
mutations.note: An `end-user` or an `entity` subject never registered a rule, so the plan is vacuous — and falling through would still ANSWER zero, because `createdBy` is NOT NULL. Only the statement count can tell the two apart, which is why it is pinned at zero.

mutations.name: M-V37 erasure: a vacuous selector costs NO statement on the scrub either
mutations.note: The same shortcut on the write half, and it matters more: the erasure path runs inside `privacy`'s transaction, so a statement per vacuous target is a statement per target on every erasure of a non-operator subject.

mutations.name: M-V38 erasure: the containment join carries the ORGANIZATION clause
mutations.note: The outermost clause. Without it the statement scrubs every matching row in the INSTALLATION, and every other assertion about the erasure still passes.

mutations.name: M-V39 erasure: the containment join carries the PROJECT clause
mutations.note: A project-level erasure that widened to the organization would scrub a second project's standing orders. It is unfalsifiable in a tenant with ONE project, which is why the harness has a COUSIN.

mutations.name: M-V40 erasure: the containment join carries the ENVIRONMENT clause
mutations.note: The narrowest clause, and the one the scenario could not see until the erasure widened in three steps rather than one.

mutations.name: M-V41 erasure: the scrub is restricted to the SUBJECT's own rows
mutations.note: An erasure that scrubbed every row in the scope would destroy the attribution of every OTHER operator's standing orders, and would report a count that looked like a thorough job.

mutations.name: M-V42 erasure: the scrub does NOT move updatedAt
mutations.note: The whole reason this write is raw SQL rather than an `updateMany`. `updatedAt` is when the standing ORDER last changed, the DOMAIN computes it, and the in-memory double leaves it alone — so a client-stamped column is a difference the differential compares verbatim.

mutations.name: M-V43 erasure: the count and the scrub agree on the level
mutations.note: The count goes through the delegate with `tenantWhere` and the scrub through a hand-written join; TWO spellings of one containment rule can drift, so the scenario asserts at every level that the number planned is the number erased.

mutations.name: M-V44 erasure: the ENVIRONMENT id is bound only when the level names it
mutations.note: The converse of M-V43: binding NULL where the level DOES name an environment widens an environment-level erasure to its whole project.

sweep: MEASURED on a real PostgreSQL, in a container, on the machine that has a
daemon. Filled in from the run; every `kills` entry is the FULL NAME of a
case this driver watched go red, copied from the run rather than predicted.
THE BASELINE IS PROVED FIRST AND THE DRIVER REFUSES TO SCORE WITHOUT IT.
Each of the six suites is run UNMUTATED and has to exit zero with a
non-zero executed case count before any mutation is applied, and a run with
no executed cases is classified VACUOUS rather than as a kill. That is the
failure tranche 1's first sweep hit, where a cleaned `dist` made every suite
